home_descriptor: A multidisciplinary designer with an eye for systems and a love for visual communication
home_learning: Now learning to build what I design
home_img_alt: Woman with curly and loose hair, smiling outdoors, with trees and sand in the background, under natural light.
about_p1: There's never been a time in my life without something in my hands: a brush, an idea, or a new way of perceiving the world.
about_p2: Creating is how I understand, process, and express my reality.
about_p3: My path has taken me through painting, sculpture, photography, philosophy, psychology, and most recently: front-end development.
about_p4: Each discipline taught me that innovation doesn't come from working harder — it comes from connecting unexpected dots and letting curiosity lead the way.
about_p5: I believe design should make people's lives better. That's why empathy and human connection are always at the core of what I do.
about_p6: I'm drawn to challenges where I can blend art and logic, analyzing every variable without losing sight of what truly matters: people.
about_p7: When I'm truly immersed in a project, I enter that deep state of flow where my mind explores hundreds of scenarios until I find a solution that feels both logical and emotionally adequate.
about_p8: I solve design problems the same way I approach a 2000-piece puzzle: study the picture on the box, trust the process, and enjoy finding where each piece belongs.
about_p9: Outside of work, I recharge through painting, puzzles, nature, and music: the things that inspire me and remind me why I create.
about_connect_desc: I love meeting people who share the same curiosity for design, creativity, and human stories. Whether you want to collaborate, chat about ideas, or just say hi - I'd love to hear from you.

zexel_title: Three users, one product, no instruction manual
zexel_subtitle: Designing a payment platform for users with radically different needs
zexel_s1_p1: Zexel Pay started from scratch — just an idea in the partners' heads. The initial challenge wasn't designing for three user types: it was that nobody had a clear picture of what they wanted to build. Three-hour meetings were a swamp of noise and actual requirements mixed together.
zexel_s1_p2: When pressure came to cram everything into a single interface for all users, I saw the problem before it happened: a platform that tries to serve everyone ends up serving no one well. I proposed separating experiences by primary task, not by abstract user type.
zexel_s1_quote: Each user had different jobs-to-be-done: companies needed to process bulk payments and consolidate invoices; influencers needed to get paid quickly with minimal effort; admins needed to oversee the entire payment flow.
zexel_s2_p1: I worked as the sole designer, connecting product, development, and marketing — each team speaking their own language. My job was to filter, translate, and bring things down to earth.
zexel_s2_p2: I designed extensive information architecture maps, user flows, and prototypes while learning Figma on the job. Within a month of joining, I was already delivering designs for the front-end team to start working from. The first stable version shipped in September.
zexel_s2_quote: I designed components as a lowest common multiple: a reusable base for all users, with per-user specifics layered on top. This unblocked a mostly junior dev team and kept design and development moving in sync.
zexel_s3_p1: Three profiles, each with access only to what they needed: companies with batch management, CSV uploads, and payment monitoring; influencers with a minimal, direct flow; admins with full visibility and permissions. The improvements that did reach production — copy corrections, flow simplification, contextual help, translation — measurably reduced human errors and left users able to anticipate where each action would take them.
zexel_s4_p1: Everything design-related, plus something that rarely shows up in portfolios: being the translation layer between teams. Business to dev, dev to marketing, stakeholder input to actionable requirements. I made prioritization calls to unblock work when direction from above wasn't clear.
zexel_s5_li2: Design reusable components with user-specific variations.
zexel_s5_li3: Balance business goals, technical constraints, and user needs.
zexel_s5_li4: Translation between teams matters as much as visual work.
zexel_s5_li5: Trust my judgment earlier, learn metrics tools sooner, polish less in early stages.
zexel_s5_li6: I blend creative and analytical thinking, see details and big picture, stay resilient, and advocate effectively.
rebrand_title: How I convinced skeptical partners to rebrand a fintech — and why they had to
rebrand_subtitle: Full rebrand for a payment platform in the influencer marketing space
rebrand_s1_p1: The company had a solid product: a payment tool for managing collaborations between brands, agencies, and influencers. The problem was that their visual identity made every ad and social post look like a scam. In an industry where credibility is everything, the brand was actively hurting the business.
rebrand_s1_quote: Nobody inside the company had identified this as a problem until I joined. Within two months as a junior UX/UI designer, I built the case and convinced the partners to explore a rebrand — despite significant initial resistance.
rebrand_s2_p1: I led a team of two design interns over three months. We researched fintech competitors, developed three distinct concepts, and I presented them with a narrative focused on business impact, not just aesthetics.
rebrand_s2_p2: The first proposals were rejected as "too bold." But the presentation did land — it convinced the partners that the current identity was a real problem. We were given one week to come back with a new proposal: same starting point, different destination. That final version was the strongest of all.
rebrand_s2_quote: Key takeaway: aim higher than you think they'll accept. Feedback always brings you down.
rebrand_s3_p1: Full visual system overhaul: scalable logo in four versions (horizontal, vertical, square, circular), web-safe color palette with defined usage percentages, typography reduced from 6–7 inconsistent fonts to 2, and a resource library for marketing. Social media and website reputation improved noticeably. The partners, who had resisted any change at the start, ended up congratulating the team.
rebrand_s4_p1: I identified the problem, built the business case, led the team, drove the process end-to-end, and created the brand guidelines and all implementation assets. I also crafted the presentation narrative — and learned that without a good story, even gold goes unnoticed.
rebrand_s5_li1: Compelling storytelling gets buy-in where good ideas alone don't.
rebrand_s5_li2: Aim higher than expected acceptance — feedback always brings you down.
rebrand_s5_li3: I over-polished early sketches fearing dismissal. I'd now trust the iterative process more.
rebrand_s5_li4: I identify problems others overlook and advocate for change despite resistance.
rebrand_s5_li5: Rejection stings but I consistently bounce back with stronger ideas.
rebrand_s5_li6: I'm capable of leadership and persuasive communication when prepared.
lightning_title: How wanting to do less work led to better results
lightning_subtitle: And taught me to redesign systems instead of pushing harder
lightning_s1_p1: Fine arts degree: dozens of simultaneous projects across painting, sculpture, photography, printmaking — each requiring finished physical work plus a full written process journal. First three years, I worked more hours than the calendar had. No Christmas break, mediocre output across the board, and a portfolio of completely unrelated pieces with no coherence.
lightning_s1_quote: The real problem wasn't the workload. It was that I was choosing each project's theme on the day I had to start it — and then brute-forcing my way through with maximum effort and no strategy.
lightning_s2_p1: In my fourth year, I stopped. Instead of launching straight into making things, I gathered every project brief from every subject and sat with them. I didn't touch a brush for weeks — well into late November — while I looked for a single underlying concept that could serve all of them at once.
lightning_s2_p2: That discomfort of not starting was real. But I pushed through it and found the thread: one conceptual project that could be adapted across all subjects and serve as the theoretical foundation for my final degree project.
lightning_s2_quote: The instinct to pause, map requirements, find the underlying structure, and design a system instead of grinding harder — that's been there since before I knew it had a name.
lightning_s3_p2: No Christmas. Scattered output. Maximum effort, mediocre results. A portfolio that said nothing coherent.
lightning_s3_p4: First Christmas in four years. Less physical work, more focused output. A cohesive body of work that fed directly into my final project.
lightning_s4_p1: I didn't learn this in a UX course. I figured it out because I was too tired to keep working the same broken way.
lightning_s4_p2: I call it the laziness lightning bolt: the moment you realize that working smarter isn't a shortcut, it's just a better way to build.
lightning_s4_p3: This is how I approach every complex problem: pause, map the requirements, find the underlying structure, then design the system.
